## Introduction

I’m a software engineer, semi-retired since February 2024\.

I’ve owned guitars since my teenage years and since the run up to entering semi-retirement I’ve spent a bit more money and time on the hobby.  One of my purchases was a Fender Mustang LT40S modelling guitar amplifier, and I discovered that there were a number of open source projects on GitHub related to the USB capabilities of this and other (older) amps under the Fender Mustang brand umbrella.

One of the projects on GitHub is called ‘plug’ and is an updated version of a software package called mustang-plug which has been part of the Debian software distribution since 2012\.  The original mustang-plug project and the more recent GitHub update are built to interoperate with Fender Mustang models released up to 2016 with model names Mustang I, II, III, IV and V.  With a lot of help from the code of a C\# GitHub project called ‘LtAmp’, I was able to make for the newer GitHub ‘plug’ codebase so that it would connect to my LT40S and download its preset definitions.  At this point I realized that without access to any of the older models plug originally served I had no way of checking whether my changes broke interoperation with the older target models (but I’m pretty certain they would have).

I decided to take the knowledge I had gained from ‘LtAmp’, ‘plug’ and my fork, and build a separate project to continue my work, which is under development at:  
[https://github.com/tim-littlefair/maneline](https://github.com/tim-littlefair/maneline).

## Components

### Fender Mustang LT40S Modelling Guitar Amplifier

![][image7]  
The amplifier is available in Australia for around AU$350-$400, and is clearly intended by Fender as a value offering to price-conscious consumers who are interested in trying a modelling amplifier but aren’t prepared to pay the price of their premium Mustang GTX- series (starting around AU$570, ).

The unit generates a solid 40W sound with good bass tones from its built-in twin 4” speakers, and is reasonably compact and portable (i.e. single-hand carry).  The ‘S’ in the model number reflects the fact that the twin-speaker arrangement enables a stereo effect.

The LT40S and other models in Fender’s LT- series group (Mustang LT25, Mustang LT50 and bass-oriented Rumble LT25) contain mathematical models of about 25 amplifiers, 25 effect pedals, and 30 factory-installed preset tones and 30 additional empty preset slots built using combinations of those mathematical models.  Each preset tone is defined by selecting one amplifier module, and up to 4 effect modules to build a pipeline to convert the raw audio from the guitar pickup to an amplified sound.

The user can switch between the 60 possible presets by rotating the rightmost cylindrical knob shown above, and preset amp and effect module selections and parameters can be changed directly from the controls on the amp.  While selecting presets is fairly easy so long as you know the numeric slot index for the target preset, personally, I do not find that editing the modules and their parameters on the amp is easy.

Fender have released software called ‘Fender Tone LT Desktop’ for macOS and Windows which use the USB interface on the amp and can be used to select and edit presets, to add additional presets beyond the 30 installed in the factory, and to backup the amp presets to servers controlled by Fender.  

The amp itself is absolutely excellent, the Fender Tone companion software frustrates me in a number of ways, including:

* While I own laptops capable of running macOS and Windows 10, my preferred home computer is a desktop machine running Ubuntu Linux 24.04 LTS, and there is no companion app for this platform.  
* It would also be nice to have a companion app version which can be run from an iOS or Android tablet (much more portable than a laptop).  
* The Fender Tone companion application does not provide any method of capturing an offline backup of preset states \- the backup can only be saved to a server controlled by Fender, and I have no guarantee that the server will still be operating if I want to restore a backup some years after making it.  
* Related to the backup concern, the current version of the companion app does not appear to make it easy to share preset definitions with other users of LT series amps.  
* While both the amp and the first party companion app allow editing the amp and effect models and their parameters, during normal operation all details of the configuration are hidden behind the numeric slot index of the preset and its name.  As a nerd, I’m quite interested in knowing for any given preset what amp and effects it is modelling, and what parameters might be available for tweaking the preset, and being able to create and compare similar presets.

### Raspberry Pi 4 hosting Maneline software

![][image8]![][image9]

See the subsection The Maneline software under development at the GitHub address scratches some of these itches sin the following ways:

* On startup, the software downloads definitions of all of all non-empty presets in the amp and stores them as human readable JSON files in the filesystem of the host device.  
* The software includes a web server which serves simple HTML pages which can be used to feed back the state of the amp and accept commands for it.

* We are seeking maker type projects (explore [published projects](https://core-electronics.com.au/projects) to get a feel of what that means). This doesn't happen often, though if it does then we will let you know why we didn't publish your project. With that in mind, store credit is not guaranteed for every submission. * We check for plagiarism in various ways, do not submit content that has been shared elsewhere which you do not have the rights to do so.

* Why did you start out on this project?

Now for the build\! It’s like writing a recipe \- describe how you built it, and be sure to hone-in on any moments that you feel other makers would find interesting. This should be 2+ vertical pages of content.

Along the way, share photos, code and the bits needed for others to do the same, or remix. Don’t stress about document styling, we will help with that after.

We’ve included some tips for writing about various types of projects on the next few pages.

Let’s get cooking\! Write out your Steps / build guide here: 

**Some Tips on Sharing Different Project Aspects with the Community**

**Sharing Code:**  
Don’t forget to add in plenty of comments to explain what your code is doing. The goal is to help others understand it, so they can learn from it, and be able to modify and remix it for their own projects.

Take a look at our [Arduino Workshop for Beginners](https://core-electronics.com.au/tutorials/arduino-workshop-for-beginners.html) \- this has some really great examples of code comments. Make sure to explain any neat tricks (eg. bitshifting or modifying registers) you’re using, or link to a resource that explains it in more detail.

If you’re comfortable with GitHub, sharing it on a GitHub repo is great\!

If you’ve used specific software libraries, don’t forget to link to the repo and/or installation instructions.

**Sharing Wiring Diagrams and Schematics:**  
A neat hand sketch is fine, but if you’re looking to take it to the next level and are happy to learn some new skills, checkout [KiCAD](https://kicad.org/) or [Fritzing](https://fritzing.org/). [Paul Falstad’s Circuit sim](https://www.falstad.com/circuit/) is also pretty neat, and has a really gentle learning curve.

Don’t forget to label your components\!

**Mechanical Details and CAD Files:**  
A neat hand drawing is fine, a 2D drawing file is better, and a CAD file that other makers can modify and remix is best. Try to avoid proprietary file formats (like .prt, or .sldprt) if possible \- universal formats like .obj, .dxf, .dwg, .stl, .igs, .step, or .pdf are best.

Even better, go open source and learn [FreeCAD](https://www.freecadweb.org/)\! It’s come along in leaps and bounds in recent years.

**3D Printing:**  
Let us know your settings \- which slicer did you use? Nozzle temps? Print speeds? Bed adhesion tricks? What printer did you use?

**Sharing Files:**  
Upload them to a cloud hosting service like Google drive and send us a link.

**Assembly and Manufacturing Instructions**  
Sequenced photos through the build process are always great. Full marks for a clear Assembly diagram of your widget.

Once again, don’t forget to checkout our guide on Photography for Makers.

Even though a picture’s worth a thousand words, sometimes it’s still not enough. For these cases when you really need a video, uploading to YouTube or another cloud hosting service is good.

**Parts List / Bill of Materials**  
Include all the main / big pieces at the top. Make sure you include links for all the major parts so others know where to get them\! If ther’s a cool bit of gear that was essential for your project, which you think we should supply, let us know and we’ll see what we can do\!

If you needed a bunch of off the shelf, jelly bean parts (resistors, capacitors, inductors, diodes, etc.) include these as CSV format bill of materials to be attached at the end.

**Planning and Calculations**  
If you needed to get your engineering hat on, let others know how you determined your requirements. Did you do some experiments/empirical testing, did you nerd out reading some academic papers or circuit theory? Let us know all about it\!
